story.title: Zelenskyy Calls for U.S. Sanctions on Russia After Trump Pauses Them
story.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged supporters to advocate for new U.S. sanctions against Russia, following President Donald Trump's decision to pause a package of sanctions aimed at the Russian economy. Trump's executive order, which he justified as being in the national interest, marks a significant shift in U.S. policy towards Russia amid deteriorating relations with Ukraine.

event_overview.title: About Russia Sanctions
event_overview.subject: Russia Sanctions
event_overview.summary: The relevant legislative event is the Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act (CAATSA), a U.S. law that created and expanded sanctions authorities concerning Iran, Russia, and North Korea. Its Russia provisions form one component of the broader U.S. Russia-sanctions framework, alongside authorities created by executive orders and other statutes.

facts.label: Legislative dates
facts.value: H.R. 3364 passed the House on July 25, 2017, passed the Senate on July 27, 2017, and became Public Law 115-44 on August 2, 2017.

facts.label: Legal scope
facts.value: CAATSA is organized into separate titles addressing Iran, the Russian Federation, and North Korea; Title II addresses Russia-related sanctions and measures concerning terrorism and illicit financing.

facts.label: Stated purpose
facts.value: The enacted law states that it provides for congressional review and counters aggression by the governments of Iran, the Russian Federation, and North Korea.

facts.label: Administration
facts.value: The Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control administers CAATSA-related sanctions; OFAC identifies CAATSA as implemented through Public Law 115-44 and Executive Order 13849.

facts.label: Relation to wider Russia sanctions
facts.value: CAATSA is not the only U.S. Russia-sanctions authority: OFAC separately lists Russian Harmful Foreign Activities and Ukraine-/Russia-related sanctions programs, among others.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline highlights particular sanctions and maritime-enforcement developments, but does not provide a complete history of U.S. Russia sanctions; its September 2026 House-passage title should not be read as the date of CAATSA’s actual 2017 congressional passage.

explore_lenses.label: What exactly did Trump’s order pause?
explore_lenses.title: New Graham Act measures were waived, not all Russia sanctions
explore_lenses.summary: The October 16 order activated tariff provisions in the new Russia-Iran law but simultaneously waived the law’s duties, sanctions, and restrictions. It explicitly preserved pre-existing Russia-related measures imposed under earlier executive orders.

claims.text: The order says the Graham Act, signed on September 18, 2026, authorized sanctions, restrictions, and duties related to Russia, and that the president waived their application after submitting a national-interest certification to Congress.

The order sets out potential 500% duties on Russian goods and 100% duties for certain purchasers of Russian oil and gas or facilitators of sanctions evasion, but makes those duties subject to the waivers.
The order states that it does not affect sanctions or other measures under the pre-existing national emergency concerning harmful Russian government activities.

points: The order says the Graham Act, signed on September 18, 2026, authorized sanctions, restrictions, and duties related to Russia, and that the president waived their application after submitting a national-interest certification to Congress.

The order sets out potential 500% duties on Russian goods and 100% duties for certain purchasers of Russian oil and gas or facilitators of sanctions evasion, but makes those duties subject to the waivers.
The order states that it does not affect sanctions or other measures under the pre-existing national emergency concerning harmful Russian government activities.
explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: The White House order says a report explaining the national-interest certification was sent to Congress, but the consulted public order does not provide that report’s detailed rationale.
explore_lenses.note: Researched context; forecasts and viewpoints are labeled and attributed.

explore_lenses.label: Why are Ukraine and Europe objecting?
explore_lenses.title: They argue pressure is needed amid attacks and winter risks
explore_lenses.summary: Zelenskyy and EU leaders link continued sanctions pressure to Russia’s ongoing war and attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. Their position conflicts with Washington’s stated determination that the statutory waivers currently serve U.S. national interests.

claims.text: Ukraine’s president told EU leaders that Russia showed no sign it was ready to end the war and urged partners not to ease sanctions while Ukraine prepares a winter package covering energy, air defense, and financing.

The European Council said Russia was continuing deliberate and systematic attacks on Ukrainian civilians and critical infrastructure, including energy systems, and called for efforts to strengthen Ukraine’s resilience before winter.

EU leaders regretted the U.S. decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel and called for coordinated further measures to reduce Russian energy revenue, close loopholes, and counter sanctions evasion.
The White House order characterizes the waivers as in the national interests of the United States, without publicly detailing the underlying certification in the order itself.

explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: The available official documents establish the competing positions but do not resolve whether the waiver will alter Russian military decisions or energy-market conditions.

explore_lenses.label: What steps are confirmed next?
explore_lenses.title: U.S. monitoring and separate EU support measures continue
explore_lenses.summary: The U.S. order creates an ongoing monitoring process and leaves the waiver reversible. Separately, the EU has committed to continued Ukraine support and further sanctions work, but no public timetable for a U.S. reversal is specified.

claims.text: The U.S. Trade Representative, working with the State, Treasury, and Energy departments, must monitor purchases of Russian oil and gas and sanctions-evasion facilitation, report regularly to the president, and flag circumstances that could warrant action on the waivers.
The waivers remain in effect until the president or the secretary of state, in consultation with relevant agencies, determines that further action is appropriate.

At its October 15-16 summit, the EU welcomed continued disbursements from its €90 billion Ukraine support loan, the release of €6.6 billion under the European Peace Facility, and an integrated anti-ballistic missile coalition.
The EU also committed to pursue further Russia measures with partners, including steps against energy revenues, sanctions loopholes, and the shadow fleet.

story_report.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged partners to press for new U.S. sanctions on Russia after President Donald Trump ordered waivers for measures targeting the Russian economy. The White House described the waivers as serving U.S. national interests, while leaving earlier Russia-related sanctions intact. The move prompted criticism from Ukrainian and EU leaders, who argue that pressure on Russian energy revenue should be maintained as Ukraine seeks support for winter energy, air-defense and financing needs.

sections.heading: Waivers Cover Russia Sanctions Law
sections.body: The executive order concerns the Graham Act, signed on September 18, 2026, which authorized sanctions, restrictions and duties related to Russia. Its potential measures include 500% duties on Russian goods and 100% duties on certain buyers of Russian oil or gas, as well as facilitators of sanctions evasion. The order makes those duties subject to waivers, while specifying that measures under the pre-existing national emergency concerning harmful Russian government activities remain unaffected.

sections.heading: Ukraine and European Union Push Back
sections.body: Zelenskyy told EU leaders that Russia had shown no sign of readiness to end the war and urged partners not to ease sanctions. The European Council said Russia continued deliberate and systematic attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure, including energy systems, and called for strengthened Ukrainian resilience before winter. EU leaders also regretted the temporary lifting of U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel and called for coordinated measures against Russian energy revenue, sanctions loopholes and evasion.

sections.heading: U.S. Agencies Monitor Russian Energy Purchases
sections.body: The U.S. trade representative, working with the State, Treasury and Energy departments, is directed to monitor purchases of Russian oil and gas and possible sanctions-evasion facilitation. The agencies must report to the president and identify conditions that could warrant action on the waivers. The waivers remain in force until the president or the secretary of state, consulting relevant agencies, determines that further action is appropriate.

unresolved.text: The public order says a report explaining the national-interest certification was sent to Congress, but does not provide the report's detailed rationale. It also sets no public deadline for reassessing or ending the waivers, and the available official documents do not establish whether they will affect Russian military decisions or energy-market conditions.

related_stories.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has condemned US President Donald Trump's decision to waive sanctions on Russia, stating it only serves to reward Vladimir Putin. Meanwhile, Russia has celebrated the waiver as a 'historic' move, raising alarms in Ukraine about the implications for their ongoing conflict.

related_stories.title: Iran Rejects Claims of Involvement in Houthi Attacks on Aden Airport
related_stories.summary: Iran has denied accusations of involvement in recent Houthi missile attacks on Saudi targets, including the international airport in Aden, Yemen. This denial follows Saudi Arabia's claims that Iran encouraged the Houthis' escalation against the kingdom. The Aden airport was struck by two missiles late on Friday, marking the second such incident in less than two weeks.
